extracted.intended_audience: scholars and researchers of media studies, computational social science, political sociology, and anyone studying protest reporting or Chinese social media
extracted.subtask_description: Systematic empirical evaluation of selection and description biases in protest reporting on Chinese Weibo by government and news media accounts, using the CASM-China protest dataset and machine learning / regression analyses. Focuses on which protests are covered and how covered (framing, sentiment, mentions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection bias (coverage rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Selection bias aims to measure “which subset of events are covered.”’ The media covers only a small, selected number of protests (selection bias).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure coverage rate as proportion of CASM protests reported by account types (e.g. government accounts covered 0.4% of protests; news media covered 6.3%). Model predictors of whether an event is covered (logistic) and how often (quasi‑Poisson). Include event and user covariates and province/year fixed effects. Interpret in light of state regulation and newsworthiness trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description bias (veracity / portrayal)
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Description bias aims to measure “the veracity of the coverage.”’ For events that are reported, portrayals may differ from how participants experience them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare characteristics extracted from individual (CASM) posts with media/government posts on action form, sentiment, police presence, and mentions of state. Identify misrepresentation (deemphasizing violence, police, negative sentiment) and framing differences. Quantify direction and magnitude of deviation from individuals' descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness factors (predictors of selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors commonly contributing to newsworthiness include spatial proximity, relation to issue attention cycles, size of the protest, violent or disruptive action, existence of counterdemonstrations, and connection to salient government/local issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include these variables as predictors in selection models; expect media to favor protests with high news value, though constrained by state pressures in China.

rubrics_metrics.name: State embeddedness / structural constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: In authoritarian settings structural factors (state regulation and influence) heavily shape selection bias; media closer to the state exhibit higher degrees of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify actors by embeddedness to the state (government accounts, government news media, commercial media, self-media) and test heterogeneous selection/description patterns across this spectrum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account typology and expected behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors on Weibo are typologized into government accounts and three types of news media: government news media, commercial media, and self-media, arrayed on a spectrum of state embeddedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use verification status and account metadata/usernames to classify accounts. Expect: government accounts—high description bias, avoid violent protests; government news media—similar to government; commercial media—intermediate; self-media—least bias and most similar to individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action form (peaceful / disruptive / violent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Action form is coded as peaceful, disruptive, or violent; violent protests involve physical conflicts with officials/police; disruptive protests involve occupying public space, blocking roads, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use action form as both a predictor of selection and an outcome for description bias comparisons (e.g. government posts eschew violent protests; news media more likely to report disruptive/violent events but may frame them differently).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protest target (state vs non-state / mediated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Target categories: against state actors (including the CCP), against non-state entities such as companies, or against non-state entities but involving government as mediator (imploring government for help).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate how target affects coverage: Chinese media may avoid reporting protests that directly target the government; government accounts more likely to report protests that implore state help or target non-state actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizer / social group of protesters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of the protesters (e.g. underprivileged groups vs urban middle class or veterans) influence coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News media gravitate toward protests by disadvantaged groups; government accounts shy away from protests organized by urban middle class and veterans (groups with strong mobilizing capacity). Include group type as predictor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiment of reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure positivity/negativity of media descriptions; government coverage tends to use a more positive tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sentiment analysis on media/government posts and compare to individual posts. Treat shifts toward more positive sentiment as evidence of description bias (depoliticization / legitimacy maintenance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention of police
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether posts mention police presence or policing actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare frequency of police mentions between individual posts and media/government posts; underreporting of police presence is a component of description bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mention of government agencies / state actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and how often media mentions government agencies in protest descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government and media may be less likely to mention government agencies, or may recast protests as government-resolved legal cases; reduced explicit mention is an indicator of depoliticization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing style: episodic vs thematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodic framing focuses on concrete acts of a specific protest; thematic framing highlights general development and underlying social tensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code framing style and compare across actors: government accounts are predicted to be more thematic (synthesis of responses), news media more episodic. Use word distributions and topic/keyword analysis to detect framing orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depoliticization / neutralizing protest claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Media construction that depoliticizes protesters’ claims, marginalizes threats to regime legitimacy, or emphasizes legal/administrative resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect depoliticization through reduced mention of systemic causes, elevated legal/administrative vocabulary (e.g. 'court','legal case','protect','according to law'), more thematic government language, and increased positive sentiment; treat as a specific form of description bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event variable construction (required covariates)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each protest: geolocation; date; account characteristics (number of followers, followees and posts); issue area; protest size; protest target; action form; police presence; sentiment of reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct these variables from CASM posts and matching media posts to use in selection and description models; document measurement decisions in appendices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-to-event matching criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Matching media posts to CASM events uses (1) account classification; (2) a first-stage classifier to remove irrelevant posts; (3) matching on same location, at least one overlapping issue, and occurrence within one week of the protest; followed by manual labeling and a Random Forest classifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply sensitivity checks (e.g. relax time window to 2/4/8 weeks). Report human-labeling match rates (47.8% on sample) and classifier performance. Acknowledge potential omissions due to keyword-based raw data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account classification method
rubrics_metrics.description: Accounts classified into five types using official verification status and usernames to determine government vs different news media types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document classification rules in supplementary appendix; rely on both verification badges and string cues in usernames; validate where possible via manual checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine classification validation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance metrics reported for classifiers: Random Forest precision = 0.89, recall = 0.76 (fivefold cross‑validation); human labelling of a subset used for training/validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report precision/recall and human-match rates; propagate classifier uncertainty into downstream inference where feasible and acknowledge machine prediction errors as limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regression modeling and inference choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Use logistic regression for binary coverage (whether covered) and quasi‑Poisson regression for count/frequency (how many times covered). Include province and year fixed effects; cluster standard errors at the provincial level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify quasi‑Poisson to allow variance > mean. Include event-level and user-level covariates. Avoid clustering with a short panel at year level to prevent finite-sample bias; discuss robustness to alternative specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keyword/omission risk and censorship evasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Raw CASM data derived from 9.5 million Weibo posts that contained 50 protest-related words; some posts use homophones or inserted characters to evade censorship and may be omitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess omission bias via random checks (authors examined 30 unmatched CASM posts and found 10% missing from raw posts due to evasive spellings). Report potential bias and attempt mitigation or sensitivity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational definitions of disruptive vs violent
rubrics_metrics.description: Violent protests: physical conflicts with government officials and/or the police. Disruptive protests: occupying buildings/land, barricading, cutting off power, sitting on roads, blocking entrances—actions that disrupt public order by occupying public space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these operational definitions for coding action form; explicitly exclude protests confined to private space from being labelled disruptive.
